concerns: Spike-in behavior may not recapitulate endogenous EVs; preserved spike-in recovery could coexist with loss of endogenous material (proposal notes this but canonical evidence does not resolve it).

Large-animal intranasal negative biodistribution (ev-driedonks-2022-macaque-biodistribution) implies that even a positive in vitro compatibility gate may not translate to detectable brain exposure—species/route clearance remains an unresolved competing explanation.

MISEV2023 supports orthogonal and protease-protection assays but does not provide quantitative thresholds or establish that detergent/protease sensitivity of capture-positive eluates correlates with in vivo potency—linkage to functional potency remains inferential and high-uncertainty.

Practical assay interferences (capture-reagent compatibility with excipients) are plausible and complex; canonical evidence recommends orthogonal controls but does not supply validated capture reagents or spike-in tracers for the proposed matrix, so substantial assay development risk remains.
conclusion: The proposal is generally supported by the cited canonical evidence: MISEV2023 justifies orthogonal controls and capture-compatibility checks, non-human-primate intranasal biodistribution (Driedonks 2022) motivates validating identity before bridging, and multiple mouse studies (Hermann 2023, Kodali 2017, Zhuang 2011) show intranasal EV-localization and model-specific functional effects that support the use of membrane-protected in vitro bioassays as a potency correlate. However key translational inferential steps remain unsupported by the supplied evidence and require explicit experimental validation before the proposed gate can be relied upon.
evidence_gap: No canonical evidence directly demonstrates that preservation of a spike-in-validated orthogonal identity signature plus detergent/protease-sensitive in vitro anti-inflammatory activity after device/formulation passage predicts (a) preserved endogenous EV surface/cargo behavior across lots or (b) in vivo brain delivery/therapeutic efficacy in large animals or humans. Also absent is empirical support that an exogenous spike-in tracer will reliably mimic endogenous EV susceptibility to formulation/device-induced damage across the proposed excipient and shear matrices.
